## Before the bench {.center}

### What T1 assumed

T1 held every bath point until the reading stopped moving, then wrote it down.

That is a *static* calibration, and it is correct — provided you always wait.

Today: what happens when you cannot wait, which is most of the time.

### The question

A sensor with a time constant $\tau$, following a temperature ramping at
$\dot T$, reads **low by $\tau\dot T$**.

For ever. Averaging does not help — it makes the wrong number more precise.

By the end of the session you will have measured $\tau$ in four media and
checked that prediction against a ramp.

## At the bench {.center}

### What you will do

1. Four plunges — still air, forced air, still water, stirred water.
2. One sheathed probe, in stirred water.
3. One ramp, with the sensor already immersed.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Three things that ruin a run

**Start recording before the plunge**, not at it: without a baseline the fit
has no $T_0$.

**Record for at least $5\tau$**, or $T_\infty$ is a guess and the fit will
trade it against $\tau$.

**Time the transfer.** The model assumes it is instantaneous. In stirred
water, where $\tau$ is seconds, it is not.
:::

### Then

Open [the handbook](handbook.qmd) and one of the analysis templates —
[Python](analysis-py.qmd) or [R](analysis-r.qmd).

Both convert volts to temperature with **your T1 calibration**, so bring it.

## What you should come away with {.center}

### Three sentences you should be able to defend

1. "This probe has $\tau = $ … in stirred water and … in still air; $\tau$
   belongs to the probe *and* the medium."
2. "A first-order fit to the sheathed probe leaves an arc-shaped residual,
   which is how you know one lump is not enough."
3. "On a bath ramping at $\dot T$, this probe reads low by $\tau\dot T$, and
   I measured that as well as predicted it."
